extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and advanced law students studying reissue and extension procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal rules governing reissue and extension of patents, the scope of permissible amendments, the deference due to the Commissioner of Patents, and what matters courts may examine in suits for infringement or direct challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive character of commissioner's decision on reissue/extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The commissioner, before granting a reissue or extension, must determine whether the defect arose from inadvertence, accident, or mistake, or from fraudulent intention; his decision is conclusive and 'not re-examinable, except, perhaps, so far as he decided there was no fraud.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In suits founded upon a reissued or extended patent, courts must presume the commissioner duly performed his duty and that the amended description is of the same invention as the original. See Rubber Company v. Goodyear; Seymour v. Osborne. A defendant sued for infringement generally may not collaterally attack the commissioner's allowance of a reissue or extension except where the commissioner exceeded his authority or fraud appears on the face of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between matters of fact and matters of construction
rubrics_metrics.description: All matters of fact connected with the surrender and reissue of a patent are conclusively settled by the decision of the commissioner; matters of construction arising on the face of the instrument remain open to court examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will treat the commissioner's factual findings as final in infringement suits, but will independently construe the patents' language. Cases: Seymour v. Osborne, Rubber Co. v. Goodyear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissued patent must be for the same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: It is clearly settled that the reissued letters-patent must be for the same invention as that embraced in the original patent; if, by comparison as a matter of law, the reissue is substantially different, it is invalid for want of jurisdiction in the commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court determines identity by comparing the two instruments (original and reissue); drawings and models filed with the original are also proper for consideration. If the commissioner exceeded authority by granting a reissue for a different invention, the reissue is void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible scope of amendments in a reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee may redescribe his invention in an amended specification and is not rigidly confined to prior wording; he may include whatever was suggested or substantially indicated in the original, provided it was properly embraced in the invention as actually made and perfected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences in description and claims are not dispositive so long as identity of the subject-matter is preserved; the description may be varied and claims restricted or enlarged within that range. The drawings and model may show what was 'substantially indicated.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on adding new, material features in a reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpolations of new features, ingredients, or devices which were neither described, suggested, nor indicated in the original patent, and which would make the reissued patent for a substantially different invention, are not allowed and will render the reissued patent void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: attempting to use reissue to claim material additions not substantially embraced in the surrendered letters-patent. Courts will invalidate such reissues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert testimony when technical terms are present
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the specification and claim (original or reissued) employ technical terms or terms of art, the court may hear testimony of scientific witnesses to aid in ascertaining the true meaning of the language employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony of scientific witnesses may be indispensable in some cases; both parties have a right to examine such witnesses and it is error to reject essential expert testimony. Cases: Bischoff v. Wethered; Betts v. Menzies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner may correct errors of his own earlier examination
rubrics_metrics.description: If an error or mistake in allowance/restriction was made by the commissioner himself (e.g., suggesting a narrowed claim), the commissioner has authority to grant a reissue correcting that error under special circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when the commissioner wrongly suggested a restricted claim and later it is discovered no legal objection existed, surrender and reissue restoring the original claim were allowed (Davidson syringe example; Morey v. Lockwood).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion to split original invention into multiple reissues
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissue that separates an original invention into two reissued patents may be held valid; some discretion must be left to the head of the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bennet v. Fowler upheld two reissues covering related aspects of the original invention. Determining whether to embrace improvements in one or multiple patents can be 'a nice and perplexing question' committed in part to Patent Office discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's duty to receive and examine applications; remedies for refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: On filing an application for a patent or reissue and payment of required duty, the commissioner must make or cause an examination and grant the patent/reissue if statutory requirements are met. If he refuses to receive an application, mandamus will lie to compel him to do so; if he refuses to grant after examination, the claimant has a statutory right of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandamus only compels the commissioner to act (receive/examine) and cannot substitute for a writ of error; where examination was refused at the threshold, courts have ordered the commissioner to examine (Commissioner of Patents v. Whiteley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary threshold questions of applicant status are for the commissioner
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions such as whether an applicant is an assignee with the required interest are 'lying at the threshold' and are for the commissioner to answer in the first instance; he must receive the application and decide on such preliminary matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the commissioner decides the applicant lacks requisite status, that decision is within his authority and review is by appeal, not by mandamus to force further examination. See Commissioner of Patents v. Whiteley.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of reissue on term and on assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: A reissued patent is granted for the unexpired term commencing from the date of the original patent (the reissue 'operates from the commencement of the original'), and will enure to the benefit of assignees who became such before the reissue even if no assignment is made after the reissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue does not create a new full term; it continues the original term for the remainder. This affects rights of assignees and infringers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may omit parts of original claims in reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutes authorizing reissue do not require the patentee to claim in his renewed patent all things claimed in his original patent; he may omit parts he deems proper and retain only such part of his original invention as he chooses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story's view: omitting portions of the original invention in a renewed patent is permissible and may even be advisable if original claims were excessive or misleading; no policy forbids restricting claims on reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and timing of extensions under the statute
rubrics_metrics.description: An extension (e.g., the seven-year extension under the 1836/1848 acts) could not be granted after the expiration of the term for which the patent was originally issued; an extension granted while the original term had not yet expired is valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrender and reissue by assignees does not necessarily defeat the original patentee's statutory right to apply for an extension. The extension takes effect in relation to the original term; courts examine whether the statutory prohibition against post-expiration extensions applies based on when the certificate was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on using fraud as a collateral defence in infringement suits
rubrics_metrics.description: After the Supreme Court's rule, a person sued as an infringer cannot abrogate a reissued or extended patent by showing it was obtained by fraud in a suit for infringement; the door is closed against showing fraud in procuring reissued or extended patents as a defence in such suits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine leaves open the possibility of impeaching a patent for fraud in a proceeding had directly for that purpose (e.g., a direct proceeding to annul the patent), but not as a collateral defence in infringement litigation. See Rubber Company v. Goodyear and subsequent cases.
